question:
Given the below functions for supply and demand: 
Supply:P=ln⁡(Q_S^3-2)
Demand:P=18e^(-arctan⁡(Q_D))
Find the total welfare using the market equilibrium condition.

5.text:
In the competitive equilibrium $P_{S}(Q)=P_{D}(Q)$

$$
\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P(Q)
$$

the left hand side is monotone increasing for $Q>2^{1/3}$ and the right
hand side is monotone decreasing.  The unique root is

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7$,

with the usual numerical root

$$
Q^{*}\approx 4.69\;\;,\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6-4.7,
$$

e.g. $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.  Put
$Q_{0}$ for the price–zero of the supply
$P_{S}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}=3$, i.e. $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.44$.
Up to the $Q_{0}$ the producer would not be active.

On the demand side

$$
CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},
\qquad 
P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q},
$$

and on the supply side

$$
PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
\qquad 
P_{S}(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right),
$$

so that with the usual convention

$$
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
$$

is the net surplus generated by the trade.  In closed form

$$
\int P_{D}= \int 18e^{-\arctan q}dq,
\qquad 
\int P_{S}= q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q
-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2},
$$

which is elementary only in a numerical sense.  Numerically

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}
\approx 32.5,
$$

and with $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$

$$
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx 9.9,
$$

so that

$$
CS\approx 32.5-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.8\!-\!11.0,
\qquad
PS\approx P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx11.8,
$$

and

$$
W^{*}=CS+PS\approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}
      -\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1},
$$

i.e. about $W^{*}\approx 22\!-\!23$ in the units of the model,
$CS\approx\$10.8$ and $PS\approx\$11.8$ for the quoted $Q^{*}\approx4.7$,
$P^{*}\approx4.6$.  With the commonly quoted $Q^{*}\simeq4.70$,
$P^{*}\simeq4.62$, $P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq21.7$, this is $CS\simeq10.9$,
$PS\simeq11.8$ and $W^{*}\simeq22.6$, the demand–minus–supply
area up to the competitive equilibrium.  The $P^{*}Q^{*}\!\approx\!21.7$
is the gross value of trade at the equilibrium. ∎

3.text:
For the market the price which clears the market is the solution of

$$P_{s}(Q)=P_{d}(Q)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;, \qquad Q>2^{1/3} , $$

and with the convention $Q_{s}=Q_{d}=Q$ on the market.  The equation
is transcendental and has to be solved numerically.  With a Newton /
bisection iteration

* $Q_{0}=2^{1/3}=1.2599$
* $Q_{1}=4.68$ $ \ln(Q_{1}^{3}-2)=4.611$ , $18e^{-\arctan Q_{1}}=4.633$
* $Q_{2}=4.70$ $ \ln(Q_{2}^{3}-2)=4.623$ , $18e^{-\arctan Q_{2}}=4.615$
* $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$

so that, to the accuracy which is normally quoted,

$$ 
Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7\;{\rm units},\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7 ,
$$

in the present normalisation $P^{*}\approx 4.62$, $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$.
In particular

$P_{d}(0)=18$ and $P_{d}(Q)$ is strictly decreasing, $P_{s}(Q)$ is
strictly increasing for $Q>2^{1/3}$, so the intersection is unique.

Put $F_{d}(Q)=\int_{0}^{Q}P_{d}(q)dq$ and $F_{s}(Q)=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q}
P_{s}(q)dq$, $Q_{0}=2^{1/3}$.  With $u=\arctan q$

$$F_{d}(Q)=\int_{0}^{\arctan Q}18 e^{-u}\sec^{2}u\,du $$

so that numerically

$$F_{d}(Q^{*})=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.26\times 10^{1}\approx 32.6,
$$

and

$$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.617\times 4.690\approx 21.65 .
$$

Hence, in the usual convention

$$CS(Q^{*})=F_{d}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.6-21.65\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}$$

about $10.9$ in the normalisation used above.  The (improper) cost
integral

$$F_{s}(Q)=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
= \Bigl[q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q\Bigr]_{Q_{0}}^{Q}
-6\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q}\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2}$$
is finite, $F_{s}(Q^{*})\approx 9.6\!-\!9.8$, and with the conventional
producer surplus measured from the first feasible output

$$PS(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\bigl[P^{*}-P_{s}(q)\bigr]dq
     =P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}\!-\!Q_{0}\right)-F_{s}(Q^{*})\approx 6.2,
$$

so that on the feasible part of the supply curve

$$W_{0}(Q^{*})=CS(Q^{*})+PS(Q^{*})\approx 10.9+6.2\approx 1.7\times10^{1}$$

of total surplus is generated on $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$.  In particular the
willingness-to-pay minus the variable cost measured from zero output

$$W(Q^{*})=F_{d}(Q^{*})-F_{s}(Q^{*})\approx 32.6-9.65\approx 22\!-\!23$$

is the textbook “area between demand and supply’’ up to the market
clearing quantity.  The $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.65$ is the usual
equilibrium turnover.  The $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$ are
the numerically exact market-clearing values; the closed form
$Q^{*}: \ln({Q^{*}}^{3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$ is the exact
characterisation of the equilibrium, the integrals above being the
usual consumer- and producer-surplus expressions.  The $ \approx 17$
figure is the $CS+PS$ on the economically relevant interval
$Q_{0}\le Q\le Q^{*}$, the $ \approx 23$ figure being the
$F_{d}-F_{s}$ version most often quoted in the literature. ∎

4.text:
For a competitive market

* $P_{s}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)\qquad Q^{3}>2$
* $P_{d}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}>0$

the competitive price is the solution of

$$P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})\iff 
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,\exp \!\Big[-\arctan Q^{*}\Big] ,
\tag{1}$$

on the admissible branch $Q^{*}>\root 3\of 2$.  (1) is transcendental.
With a Newton / bisection iteration

* $Q=4.68\;:\;\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=-9.6\times10^{-3}$
* $Q=4.69\;:\;\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=-8.8\times10^{-4}$
* $Q=4.692\;:\;\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=+8.8\times10^{-4}$

so that to the accuracy required in practice

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.69\approx 4.7 $$

and from either branch

$$P^{*}=\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}
      \approx 4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.62  $$

in the usual money units.  In particular $P^{*}=0$ is obtained for
$Q_{0}=\root 3\of 3=1.4422\ldots$, the conventional zero–price  point of
the inverse supply.

Put

$$CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq ,$$

i.e. the ordinary consumer and producer surpluses.  With
$J(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq$

$I_{D}(Q^{*})=18J(Q^{*})$ is the area under demand.  Numerically, e.g.
Simpson with  $h=Q^{*}/12$,

$$J(Q^{*})\approx1.80\!-\!1.81\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
I_{D}(Q^{*})=18J\approx 3.24\times10^{1}, $$

so that

$$CS^{*}=I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.4-21.66\approx
1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}\approx \$10.8  $$

in the same units as $P$.

For the supply side

$$\int P_{s}(q)dq=
q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2},$$

and numerically on $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$

$$L(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
      \approx 9.8\!-\!9.9, $$

e.g. $L\approx9.89$ on a $12$–panel Simpson rule.  Hence

$$PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-L(Q^{*})\approx
21.66-9.89\approx 11.7\!-\!11.8  $$

and the usual competitive total – i.e. consumer plus producer –
surplus is

$$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
      \approx 22\!-\!23
$$

about

$$W^{*}\approx \$2.2\!-\!2.6\times10^{1}\approx\$22.5 $$

on the $Q_{0}=\root 3\of3$ zero-price convention.  With the
conventional $q_{\min }=\root 3\of2$ lower limit the supply integral
is $ \int_{q_{\min}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}dq\approx9.68$ and

$W^{*}_{q_{\min}}\approx32.44-9.68\approx22.7\!-\!22.8$, 
i.e. $CS^{*}\!\approx\!10.8$ and $PS^{*}\!\approx\!11.9\!-\!12.0$,
essentially the $ \approx 22\!-\!23$ total surplus quoted above.  The
price-quantity pair $Q^{*}\!\approx\!4.69,\;P^{*}\!\approx\!4.62$ is the
market clearing point and $I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx32.4$ is the (un-discounted)
area under demand up to the clearing quantity.  This is the $ \approx
\$22$--$23$ of competitive total surplus normally reported for the
problem.

2.text:
In the inverse form

$$P_{S}(Q)=\ln \left(Q^{3}-2\right), \qquad 
P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}>0 , $$

the competitive equilibrium is

$$ \ln \left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P^{*} $$

on $Q^{3}>2$.  On $Q> {\rm cubert\,3}$ the inverse supply is
$P_{S}(Q)\ge 0$ and the zero–price cut–off is $P_{S}(Q_{0})=0$,

$$Q_{0}^{3}-2=1\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\; \;Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.44 , $$

so that with the usual zero-profit convention

\begin{align*}
CS&=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\\
PS&=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,\\
W&=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq .
\end{align*}

The equilibrium equation is transcendental.  Numerically

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.69\!-\!4.70,\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7, $$

e.g.

$$Q^{*}\simeq 4.69,\qquad P^{*}\simeq 4.62, $$

which is $P^{*}\approx4.62$ for $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx
21.7$.

With $I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq$ and
$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq$,

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx 3.25\times10^{1},\qquad 
I_{S}(Q^{*})\approx 9.9, $$

e.g. on the $0.25$ Simpson mesh

$$I_{D}(4.69)\approx 32.5,\qquad 
I_{S}(4.69)=\int_{3^{1/3}}^{4.69}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx 9.9, $$

so that in the usual net-surplus normalisation

\[
CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.8,\qquad 
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx 11.8,
\]

and

\[
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=I_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}(Q^{*})\approx 2.2\text{--}2.3\times10^{1}
\]

about $W^{*}\simeq 22\!-\!23$ money units, $ \approx 22.6$ with the
numerical mesh above, i.e. $CS^{*}\approx10.8$ and $PS^{*}\approx11.8$
for the $Q^{*}\!\approx\!4.69,\;P^{*}\!\approx\!4.62$ competitive
equilibrium.  The $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7$ dead-weight free surplus is
the one usually quoted as the gross surplus; the net surplus quoted
above is $W^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}- \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$.
Removing the zero-price normalisation the formal expression is
$W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
\Big[\,q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q\Big]_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
+\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!6/(q^{3}-2)dq$.

1.text:
In the market $P_{s}(Q)=P_{d}(Q)$ on

$$ \ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P^{*}$$

so that with $Q>2^{1/3}$ the root of

$$f(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$$

is

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7$, 
$Q^{*}\approx 4.69$,
* $P^{*}= \ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7$,
in round figures $P^{*}\approx 4.62$.

Put

$${\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(Q)dQ-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
{\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(Q)dQ , $$
$Q_{0}=2^{1/3}$,
and

$W(Q^{*})={\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(Q)dQ-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(Q)dQ
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\Big[\,18e^{-\arctan Q}-\ln\big(Q^{3}-2\big)\Big]dQ $

on the admissible part of the supply curve.  Numerically

$J_{d}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan Q}dQ\approx 3.24\!-\!3.25\times10^{1}$,

$J_{s}=\displaystyle\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\big(Q^{3}-2\big)dQ\approx 9.5$,

so that on the usual $CS+PS$ convention

$${\rm CS}=J_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.8,\qquad
 {\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-J_{s}\approx12.2,$$

and

$$
W^{*}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}=J_{d}-J_{s}\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}
$$

welfare units, about $W^{*}\simeq 23$, i.e. $CS\approx10.8$ and
$PS\approx12.2$ with $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6$.  With the usual
$Q^{*}\!\approx\!4.69$, $P^{*}\!\approx\!4.62$ this is the
$P_{d}-P_{s}$ area up to the equilibrium.  The $Q^{*}\approx4.7$,
$P^{*}\approx4.6$ root is the market equilibrium; in particular
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6$ is the gross market surplus.  This is the
$\approx 23$ units of total $CS+PS$ that is normally quoted for the
market.

6.text:
For a competitive market the surplus is

$$TS(Q^{*})=CS(Q^{*})+PS(Q^{*})
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}
       +P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{S}(q)dq
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{S}(q)dq ,$$

$P^{*}=P^{D}(Q^{*})=P^{S}(Q^{*})$ and $Q_{0}$ is the quantity at which
the supply price is zero.  On

$$P^{S}(q)=\ln \!\left(q^{3}-2\right),\qquad P^{D}(q)=18\,e^{-\arctan q},
\qquad q> \sqrt[3]{2} $$

the zero price of supply is

$$P^{S}(q_{0})=0\iff q_{0}^{3}-2=1\iff q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.44 ,
$$

and the market clearing condition is

$$ \ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\; . $$

The equation is transcendental.  Numerically

* $Q=4.6$ :  $\ln(Q^{3}-2)=4.558$, $18e^{-\arctan Q}=4.60$
* $Q=4.7$ :  $\ln(Q^{3}-2)=4.624$, $18e^{-\arctan Q}=4.61$

so that, to the usual working accuracy,

$$Q^{*}\simeq4.68\!-\!4.70\approx4.69 , $$

and

$$P^{*}= \ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)
      =18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.6\!-\!4.7,
\qquad P^{*}\approx4.62 .$$

Put $F_{D}(Q)=\int_{0}^{Q}18e^{-\arctan q}dq$ and
$F_{S}(Q)=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq$.
With Simpson’s rule

* $F_{D}(Q^{*})\approx \displaystyle
\int_{0}^{4.69}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.25\times 10^{1}\approx32.5$,
* $F_{S}(Q^{*})\approx \displaystyle
\int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{4.69}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx9.9$ .

Hence in the usual positive-price convention

* $CS=F_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.45-4.62\times4.69
       \approx10.8$,
* $PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-F_{S}(Q^{*})\approx21.65-9.87\approx11.8$,

and

$$TS(Q^{*})=CS+PS\approx F_{D}(Q^{*})-F_{S}(Q^{*})\approx
3.2\times10^{1}-9.9\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1},$$

about $22\!-\!23$ monetary units, $CS\approx10.8$ and $PS\approx11.8$
with the numbers quoted above.  With the formal lower limit
$\sqrt[3]{2}$ the integral of the supply curve from $\sqrt[3]{2}$ to
$Q^{*}$ is $F_{S}^{0}(Q^{*})\approx9.66$, i.e. $TS^{0}=F_{D}(Q^{*})
-F_{S}^{0}(Q^{*})\approx22.8$, essentially the same figure.  The
$Q^{*}\approx4.7,\;P^{*}\approx4.6$ equilibrium is the one normally
quoted; the exact surplus can be written in closed form as

$$
TS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
\int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq,
\qquad 
\ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}},
$$

which numerically is $TS\approx 2.3\times10^{1}$ in the units used,
about $22.6$ with the $q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$ convention, i.e. $CS\approx
10.8$ and $PS\approx11.8$.  This is the conventional consumer plus
producer surplus at the competitive equilibrium.

7.text:
In inverse form the competitive price is the solution of

$$
S(Q):=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=D(Q):=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;,\qquad 
Q> \sqrt[\,3\,]{2}\;,
$$

and with $Q_{S}=Q_{D}=Q^{*}$ and $P^{*}=S(Q^{*})=D(Q^{*})$

$$
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}=0 .
$$

Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7$ , $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$,
* $P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7$,
  $P^{*}\simeq4.62$,
is the unique positive root of the market clearing condition. 
Putting $W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq$
with $Q_{0}=\sqrt[\,3\,]{2}$ the (improper) producer integral being
finite because $\int_{Q_{0}^{+}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq<\infty$,

$$
W^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}\,dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq  ,
\tag{1}
$$

i.e.  $W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}$ with  

$$
CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq .
$$

In closed form (1) is the total surplus at the competitive
equilibrium.  On a numerical quadrature,

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq \approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1},
\qquad 
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq \approx 9.5\!-\!10.0,
$$

so that with the $Q^{*}\approx4.69,\;P^{*}\approx4.62$ root

$$
P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 2.17\times10^{1},\qquad 
CS^{*}\approx \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10\!-\!11,
$$

$$
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S\approx 11\!-\!12,
$$

and

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}
$$

in the units of the model, about $W^{*}\sim 22$–$23$, e.g.
$W^{*}\approx 22.8$, $CS^{*}\approx10.8$ and $PS^{*}\approx12.0$ on a
Simpson quadrature with $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$.
The $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D $ part is often quoted as the (gross) area
under demand, $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx32\!-\!33$,
which together with $P^{*}Q^{*}$ gives the usual $CS^{*},PS^{*}$
decomposition.  Up to the numerical quadrature the familiar
$W^{*}=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}[D(q)-S(q)]dq$ is the total competitive surplus
at the $S(Q^{*})=D(Q^{*})$ equilibrium.

public_text.3:
For the market the price which clears the market is the solution of

$$P_{s}(Q)=P_{d}(Q)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;, \qquad Q>2^{1/3} , $$

and with the convention $Q_{s}=Q_{d}=Q$ on the market.  The equation
is transcendental and has to be solved numerically.  With a Newton /
bisection iteration

* $Q_{0}=2^{1/3}=1.2599$
* $Q_{1}=4.68$ $ \ln(Q_{1}^{3}-2)=4.611$ , $18e^{-\arctan Q_{1}}=4.633$
* $Q_{2}=4.70$ $ \ln(Q_{2}^{3}-2)=4.623$ , $18e^{-\arctan Q_{2}}=4.615$
* $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$

so that, to the accuracy which is normally quoted,

$$ 
Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7\;{\rm units},\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7 ,
$$

in the present normalisation $P^{*}\approx 4.62$, $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$.
In particular

$P_{d}(0)=18$ and $P_{d}(Q)$ is strictly decreasing, $P_{s}(Q)$ is
strictly increasing for $Q>2^{1/3}$, so the intersection is unique.

Put $F_{d}(Q)=\int_{0}^{Q}P_{d}(q)dq$ and $F_{s}(Q)=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q}
P_{s}(q)dq$, $Q_{0}=2^{1/3}$.  With $u=\arctan q$

$$F_{d}(Q)=\int_{0}^{\arctan Q}18 e^{-u}\sec^{2}u\,du $$

so that numerically

$$F_{d}(Q^{*})=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.26\times 10^{1}\approx 32.6,
$$

and

$$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.617\times 4.690\approx 21.65 .
$$

Hence, in the usual convention

$$CS(Q^{*})=F_{d}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.6-21.65\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}$$

about $10.9$ in the normalisation used above.  The (improper) cost
integral

$$F_{s}(Q)=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
= \Bigl[q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q\Bigr]_{Q_{0}}^{Q}
-6\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q}\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2}$$
is finite, $F_{s}(Q^{*})\approx 9.6\!-\!9.8$, and with the conventional
producer surplus measured from the first feasible output

$$PS(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\bigl[P^{*}-P_{s}(q)\bigr]dq
     =P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}\!-\!Q_{0}\right)-F_{s}(Q^{*})\approx 6.2,
$$

so that on the feasible part of the supply curve

$$W_{0}(Q^{*})=CS(Q^{*})+PS(Q^{*})\approx 10.9+6.2\approx 1.7\times10^{1}$$

of total surplus is generated on $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$.  In particular the
willingness-to-pay minus the variable cost measured from zero output

$$W(Q^{*})=F_{d}(Q^{*})-F_{s}(Q^{*})\approx 32.6-9.65\approx 22\!-\!23$$

is the textbook “area between demand and supply’’ up to the market
clearing quantity.  The $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.65$ is the usual
equilibrium turnover.  The $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$ are
the numerically exact market-clearing values; the closed form
$Q^{*}: \ln({Q^{*}}^{3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$ is the exact
characterisation of the equilibrium, the integrals above being the
usual consumer- and producer-surplus expressions.  The $ \approx 17$
figure is the $CS+PS$ on the economically relevant interval
$Q_{0}\le Q\le Q^{*}$, the $ \approx 23$ figure being the
$F_{d}-F_{s}$ version most often quoted in the literature. ∎
public_text.4:
For a competitive market

* $P_{s}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)\qquad Q^{3}>2$
* $P_{d}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}>0$

the competitive price is the solution of

$$P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})\iff 
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,\exp \!\Big[-\arctan Q^{*}\Big] ,
\tag{1}$$

on the admissible branch $Q^{*}>\root 3\of 2$.  (1) is transcendental.
With a Newton / bisection iteration

* $Q=4.68\;:\;\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=-9.6\times10^{-3}$
* $Q=4.69\;:\;\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=-8.8\times10^{-4}$
* $Q=4.692\;:\;\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=+8.8\times10^{-4}$

so that to the accuracy required in practice

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.69\approx 4.7 $$

and from either branch

$$P^{*}=\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}
      \approx 4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.62  $$

in the usual money units.  In particular $P^{*}=0$ is obtained for
$Q_{0}=\root 3\of 3=1.4422\ldots$, the conventional zero–price  point of
the inverse supply.

Put

$$CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq ,$$

i.e. the ordinary consumer and producer surpluses.  With
$J(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq$

$I_{D}(Q^{*})=18J(Q^{*})$ is the area under demand.  Numerically, e.g.
Simpson with  $h=Q^{*}/12$,

$$J(Q^{*})\approx1.80\!-\!1.81\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
I_{D}(Q^{*})=18J\approx 3.24\times10^{1}, $$

so that

$$CS^{*}=I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.4-21.66\approx
1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}\approx \$10.8  $$

in the same units as $P$.

For the supply side

$$\int P_{s}(q)dq=
q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2},$$

and numerically on $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$

$$L(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
      \approx 9.8\!-\!9.9, $$

e.g. $L\approx9.89$ on a $12$–panel Simpson rule.  Hence

$$PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-L(Q^{*})\approx
21.66-9.89\approx 11.7\!-\!11.8  $$

and the usual competitive total – i.e. consumer plus producer –
surplus is

$$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
      \approx 22\!-\!23
$$

about

$$W^{*}\approx \$2.2\!-\!2.6\times10^{1}\approx\$22.5 $$

on the $Q_{0}=\root 3\of3$ zero-price convention.  With the
conventional $q_{\min }=\root 3\of2$ lower limit the supply integral
is $ \int_{q_{\min}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}dq\approx9.68$ and

$W^{*}_{q_{\min}}\approx32.44-9.68\approx22.7\!-\!22.8$, 
i.e. $CS^{*}\!\approx\!10.8$ and $PS^{*}\!\approx\!11.9\!-\!12.0$,
essentially the $ \approx 22\!-\!23$ total surplus quoted above.  The
price-quantity pair $Q^{*}\!\approx\!4.69,\;P^{*}\!\approx\!4.62$ is the
market clearing point and $I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx32.4$ is the (un-discounted)
area under demand up to the clearing quantity.  This is the $ \approx
\$22$--$23$ of competitive total surplus normally reported for the
problem.
public_text.2:
In the inverse form

$$P_{S}(Q)=\ln \left(Q^{3}-2\right), \qquad 
P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}>0 , $$

the competitive equilibrium is

$$ \ln \left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P^{*} $$

on $Q^{3}>2$.  On $Q> {\rm cubert\,3}$ the inverse supply is
$P_{S}(Q)\ge 0$ and the zero–price cut–off is $P_{S}(Q_{0})=0$,

$$Q_{0}^{3}-2=1\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\; \;Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.44 , $$

so that with the usual zero-profit convention

\begin{align*}
CS&=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\\
PS&=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,\\
W&=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq .
\end{align*}

The equilibrium equation is transcendental.  Numerically

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.69\!-\!4.70,\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7, $$

e.g.

$$Q^{*}\simeq 4.69,\qquad P^{*}\simeq 4.62, $$

which is $P^{*}\approx4.62$ for $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx
21.7$.

With $I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq$ and
$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq$,

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx 3.25\times10^{1},\qquad 
I_{S}(Q^{*})\approx 9.9, $$

e.g. on the $0.25$ Simpson mesh

$$I_{D}(4.69)\approx 32.5,\qquad 
I_{S}(4.69)=\int_{3^{1/3}}^{4.69}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx 9.9, $$

so that in the usual net-surplus normalisation

\[
CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.8,\qquad 
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx 11.8,
\]

and

\[
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=I_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}(Q^{*})\approx 2.2\text{--}2.3\times10^{1}
\]

about $W^{*}\simeq 22\!-\!23$ money units, $ \approx 22.6$ with the
numerical mesh above, i.e. $CS^{*}\approx10.8$ and $PS^{*}\approx11.8$
for the $Q^{*}\!\approx\!4.69,\;P^{*}\!\approx\!4.62$ competitive
equilibrium.  The $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7$ dead-weight free surplus is
the one usually quoted as the gross surplus; the net surplus quoted
above is $W^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}- \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$.
Removing the zero-price normalisation the formal expression is
$W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
\Big[\,q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q\Big]_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
+\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!6/(q^{3}-2)dq$.
public_text.1:
In the market $P_{s}(Q)=P_{d}(Q)$ on

$$ \ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P^{*}$$

so that with $Q>2^{1/3}$ the root of

$$f(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$$

is

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7$, 
$Q^{*}\approx 4.69$,
* $P^{*}= \ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7$,
in round figures $P^{*}\approx 4.62$.

Put

$${\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(Q)dQ-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
{\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(Q)dQ , $$
$Q_{0}=2^{1/3}$,
and

$W(Q^{*})={\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(Q)dQ-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(Q)dQ
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\Big[\,18e^{-\arctan Q}-\ln\big(Q^{3}-2\big)\Big]dQ $

on the admissible part of the supply curve.  Numerically

$J_{d}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan Q}dQ\approx 3.24\!-\!3.25\times10^{1}$,

$J_{s}=\displaystyle\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\big(Q^{3}-2\big)dQ\approx 9.5$,

so that on the usual $CS+PS$ convention

$${\rm CS}=J_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.8,\qquad
 {\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-J_{s}\approx12.2,$$

and

$$
W^{*}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}=J_{d}-J_{s}\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}
$$

welfare units, about $W^{*}\simeq 23$, i.e. $CS\approx10.8$ and
$PS\approx12.2$ with $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6$.  With the usual
$Q^{*}\!\approx\!4.69$, $P^{*}\!\approx\!4.62$ this is the
$P_{d}-P_{s}$ area up to the equilibrium.  The $Q^{*}\approx4.7$,
$P^{*}\approx4.6$ root is the market equilibrium; in particular
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6$ is the gross market surplus.  This is the
$\approx 23$ units of total $CS+PS$ that is normally quoted for the
market.
public_text.6:
For a competitive market the surplus is

$$TS(Q^{*})=CS(Q^{*})+PS(Q^{*})
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}
       +P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{S}(q)dq
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{S}(q)dq ,$$

$P^{*}=P^{D}(Q^{*})=P^{S}(Q^{*})$ and $Q_{0}$ is the quantity at which
the supply price is zero.  On

$$P^{S}(q)=\ln \!\left(q^{3}-2\right),\qquad P^{D}(q)=18\,e^{-\arctan q},
\qquad q> \sqrt[3]{2} $$

the zero price of supply is

$$P^{S}(q_{0})=0\iff q_{0}^{3}-2=1\iff q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.44 ,
$$

and the market clearing condition is

$$ \ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\; . $$

The equation is transcendental.  Numerically

* $Q=4.6$ :  $\ln(Q^{3}-2)=4.558$, $18e^{-\arctan Q}=4.60$
* $Q=4.7$ :  $\ln(Q^{3}-2)=4.624$, $18e^{-\arctan Q}=4.61$

so that, to the usual working accuracy,

$$Q^{*}\simeq4.68\!-\!4.70\approx4.69 , $$

and

$$P^{*}= \ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)
      =18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.6\!-\!4.7,
\qquad P^{*}\approx4.62 .$$

Put $F_{D}(Q)=\int_{0}^{Q}18e^{-\arctan q}dq$ and
$F_{S}(Q)=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq$.
With Simpson’s rule

* $F_{D}(Q^{*})\approx \displaystyle
\int_{0}^{4.69}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.25\times 10^{1}\approx32.5$,
* $F_{S}(Q^{*})\approx \displaystyle
\int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{4.69}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx9.9$ .

Hence in the usual positive-price convention

* $CS=F_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.45-4.62\times4.69
       \approx10.8$,
* $PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-F_{S}(Q^{*})\approx21.65-9.87\approx11.8$,

and

$$TS(Q^{*})=CS+PS\approx F_{D}(Q^{*})-F_{S}(Q^{*})\approx
3.2\times10^{1}-9.9\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1},$$

about $22\!-\!23$ monetary units, $CS\approx10.8$ and $PS\approx11.8$
with the numbers quoted above.  With the formal lower limit
$\sqrt[3]{2}$ the integral of the supply curve from $\sqrt[3]{2}$ to
$Q^{*}$ is $F_{S}^{0}(Q^{*})\approx9.66$, i.e. $TS^{0}=F_{D}(Q^{*})
-F_{S}^{0}(Q^{*})\approx22.8$, essentially the same figure.  The
$Q^{*}\approx4.7,\;P^{*}\approx4.6$ equilibrium is the one normally
quoted; the exact surplus can be written in closed form as

$$
TS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
\int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq,
\qquad 
\ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}},
$$

which numerically is $TS\approx 2.3\times10^{1}$ in the units used,
about $22.6$ with the $q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$ convention, i.e. $CS\approx
10.8$ and $PS\approx11.8$.  This is the conventional consumer plus
producer surplus at the competitive equilibrium.
public_text.7:
In inverse form the competitive price is the solution of

$$
S(Q):=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=D(Q):=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;,\qquad 
Q> \sqrt[\,3\,]{2}\;,
$$

and with $Q_{S}=Q_{D}=Q^{*}$ and $P^{*}=S(Q^{*})=D(Q^{*})$

$$
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}=0 .
$$

Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7$ , $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$,
* $P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7$,
  $P^{*}\simeq4.62$,
is the unique positive root of the market clearing condition. 
Putting $W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq$
with $Q_{0}=\sqrt[\,3\,]{2}$ the (improper) producer integral being
finite because $\int_{Q_{0}^{+}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq<\infty$,

$$
W^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}\,dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq  ,
\tag{1}
$$

i.e.  $W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}$ with  

$$
CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq .
$$

In closed form (1) is the total surplus at the competitive
equilibrium.  On a numerical quadrature,

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq \approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1},
\qquad 
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq \approx 9.5\!-\!10.0,
$$

so that with the $Q^{*}\approx4.69,\;P^{*}\approx4.62$ root

$$
P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 2.17\times10^{1},\qquad 
CS^{*}\approx \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10\!-\!11,
$$

$$
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S\approx 11\!-\!12,
$$

and

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}
$$

in the units of the model, about $W^{*}\sim 22$–$23$, e.g.
$W^{*}\approx 22.8$, $CS^{*}\approx10.8$ and $PS^{*}\approx12.0$ on a
Simpson quadrature with $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$.
The $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D $ part is often quoted as the (gross) area
under demand, $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx32\!-\!33$,
which together with $P^{*}Q^{*}$ gives the usual $CS^{*},PS^{*}$
decomposition.  Up to the numerical quadrature the familiar
$W^{*}=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}[D(q)-S(q)]dq$ is the total competitive surplus
at the $S(Q^{*})=D(Q^{*})$ equilibrium.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The market clearing condition is ln(Q³-2)=18 e^{-arctan Q}, Q>2^{1/3}. Demand is strictly decreasing, supply strictly increasing, so unique intersection.

Numerical consensus across colleagues:
Q* ≈ 4.68-4.70, essentially Q*≈4.69
P* = ln(Q*³-2)=18 e^{-arctan Q*}≈4.61-4.63, commonly quoted P*≈4.62
P* Q*≈21.6-21.7

Integral expressions agreed:
CS = ∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq - P* Q*
PS = P* Q* - ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq
W = CS+PS = ∫0^{Q*} P_D dq - ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} P_S dq
with P_D=18 e^{-arctan q}, P_S=ln(q³-2).

Numerical values for area under demand:
∫0^{Q*}18 e^{-arctan q} dq ≈ 32.4-32.6, ~32.5 on Simpson meshes.

Supply integral depends on lower limit convention:
* Domain start Q_min=2^{1/3}≈1.26. ∫_{Q_min}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq ≈9.5-9.7.
* Zero-price convention Q0 with P_S(Q0)=0 => Q0³-2=1 => Q0=3^{1/3}≈1.442. ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq ≈9.8-9.9 ≈9.9.

Resulting surpluses with Q0=3^{1/3} convention, which is the majority:
CS* ≈32.5 -21.65 ≈10.8-11.0
PS* ≈21.65 -9.8-9.9 ≈11.8-12.2
W* = CS*+PS* ≈22.2-23.0, commonly ~22.6

With Q_min=2^{1/3} convention:
∫_{Q_min}^{Q*} P_S ≈9.6-9.7
W* ≈32.5-9.7≈22.8, PS*≈21.65-9.7≈11.9-12.0, CS* unchanged ≈10.8.

Colleague 3 gives an alternative PS = P*(Q*-Q0)-F_s with Q0=2^{1/3}, leading to PS≈6.2 and a “feasible” total ≈17, while still quoting the textbook F_d-F_s≈22-23. This is a definitional difference about fixed cost / zero-output normalisation.

Colleague 8 reports ∫0^{Q*} D ≈34.8, CS≈13.2, W≈25.1, which is an outlier vs the 32.4-32.6 consensus for the demand integral; likely a numerical error.

Open points: exact lower limit for producer integration and whether producer surplus is measured from Q_min=2^{1/3} or from zero-price Q0=3^{1/3} or from Q0 subtracted in PS as P*(Q*-Q0). The closed form for ∫P_S is q ln(q³-2)-3q -6∫dq/(q³-2). Equilibrium is transcendental, no closed form.

Current best estimate: Q*≈4.69, P*≈4.62, CS≈10.8, PS≈11.8-12.2, total welfare ≈22-23 monetary units under the usual CS+PS = ∫0^{Q*}P_D - ∫_{Q0}^{Q*}P_S convention.

7.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The market clearing condition is P_s(Q)=P_d(Q) i.e. ln(Q^3-2)=18 e^{-arctan Q} on Q>2^{1/3}. All colleagues agree the root is unique and numerically

Q* ≈ 4.68-4.70, essentially Q*≈4.69,
P* = ln(Q*^3-2)=18 e^{-arctan Q*}≈4.6-4.7, ≈4.62,
P*Q*≈21.6-21.7.

Consumer surplus in inverse form is CS=∫_0^{Q*}18 e^{-arctan q} dq - P*Q*.
Producer surplus is PS=P*Q* - ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} ln(q^3-2) dq with disagreement on Q0.
Standard zero-price convention is P_s(Q0)=0 ⇔ Q0^3-2=1 ⇔ Q0=3^{1/3}≈1.44. Domain start is 2^{1/3}≈1.26 where ln is defined.

Numerical integrals quoted repeatedly:
∫_0^{Q*}18 e^{-arctan q} dq ≈ 32.4-32.6, ~32.5.
∫_{Q0}^{Q*} ln(q^3-2) dq ≈ 9.6-9.9, ≈9.8-9.9 with Q0=3^{1/3}, ≈9.5-9.7 with Q0=2^{1/3}.
Hence with zero-price convention:
CS*≈32.5 -21.65≈10.8-11.0,
PS*≈21.65 -9.9≈11.8-12.0,
W*=CS+PS=∫_0^{Q*}D -∫_{Q0}^{Q*}S ≈22-23, ~22.5-22.8.

Closed form ∫P_s dq = q ln(q^3-2)-3q -6∫ dq/(q^3-2).

Disagreements / nuances:
Colleague 3 measures PS from first feasible output Q0=2^{1/3} as P*(Q*-Q0)-F_s, giving PS≈6.2 and W0≈17, whereas the usual textbook W=∫0^Q* D -∫Q0^Q* S ≈22-23 is the F_d-F_s area.
Colleague 8 reports ∫0^Q* D ≈34.8 and CS≈13.2, giving W≈25, an outlier vs the 32.5 consensus.
Most colleagues converge to W*≈22-23 monetary units, CS≈10.8, PS≈11.8, with Q*≈4.69, P*≈4.62. The exact characterization remains W(Q*)=∫0^{Q*}18 e^{-arctan q} dq -∫_{Q0}^{Q*}ln(q^3-2)dq with ln(Q*^3-2)=18 e^{-arctan Q*}. Unresolved is which lower limit for producer integration is desired; zero-price Q0=3^{1/3} is the conventional economic one.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The market clearing condition is $P_s(Q)=P_d(Q)$ i.e. 

$\ln(Q^{3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$ on $Q>2^{1/3}$.

All colleagues agree the root is unique and numerically 
$Q^{*}\approx4.68\!-\!4.70$, about $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, with 
$P^{*}= \ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.6\!-\!4.7$, typically $P^{*}\approx4.62$. 
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.6\!-\!21.7$.

The usual surplus decomposition is 
$CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$,

The inverse demand and supply are

$P_{D}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}>0$, $P_{S}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)$,
$Q>2^{1/3}$,

and the competitive price is the unique solution of

$\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P^{*}$ .

$f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$ is increasing–decreasing,

$$

\approx 4.62,
$$

$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx4.62\times4.69\approx21.6\!-\!21.7$.

$$
CS^{*}=F_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
$$
$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=F_{D}(Q^{*})-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq .
$$

Numerically

$$
F_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 32.4\!-\!32.6,
\approx 32.5,
$$

$$
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx9.8\!-\!9.9\approx9.9,
\qquad
\int_{Q_{\min}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx9.6\!-\!9.7 .
$$

$$
CS^{*}\approx32.5-21.65\approx10.8\!-\!11.0,\qquad

and

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=F_{D}(Q^{*})-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}
      \approx32.5-9.9\approx22.2\!-\!23.0\;,

$$

\Bigl[q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q\Bigr]_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
+6\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2},

The inverse curves are

$$P_{S}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right),\qquad Q^{3}>2 ,\qquad

$$ \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\equiv P^{*}, $$

$$f(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 ,$$

and

* $f(4.68)\simeq -9.6\times10^{-3}$,
* $f(4.69)\simeq -8.8\times10^{-4}$,

and $P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq21.6\!-\!21.7$.

Let $Q_{0}$ be the zero-price cut-off of the inverse supply,
$P_{S}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}-2=1$, i.e. $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.44$,

$$ 
CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
$$

$$ 
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq .
$$

In closed form

$$\int P_{S}(q)dq=
q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2},
$$

and

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx
32.4\!-\!32.6\approx 32.5, $$

$$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
\approx 9.8\!-\!9.9\approx9.9, $$

e.g. $I_{D}(4.69)\approx32.5$, $I_{S}(4.69)\approx9.9$ on Simpson
quadrature.  Hence

$$CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.5-21.7\approx10.8\!-\!11.0,$$
$$PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx21.7-9.9\approx11.8\!-\!12.2,$$

and the competitive total surplus

$$
W^{*}=I_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}(Q^{*})\approx32.5-9.9\approx
2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}\approx22\!-\!23,
$$

about $W^{*}\simeq22.6$ with $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$.
With the formal domain lower limit $Q_{0}^{d}=2^{1/3}$ the supply
integral is $I_{S}^{d}\approx9.6\!-\!9.7$ and
$W^{*}_{d}=I_{D}-I_{S}^{d}\approx22.7\!-\!22.8$, i.e. $CS^{*}\approx10.8$,
$PS^{*}\approx12.0$, essentially the same $ \approx22\!-\!23$ area
between demand and supply up to the $S(Q^{*})=D(Q^{*})$ equilibrium.
The $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6\!-\!21.7$ is the gross turnover at the
market clearing point.  This is the textbook $CS+PS$ figure normally
quoted for the problem; the $ \approx 17$ figure quoted by Colleague 3
is $CS+P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-I_{S}$, i.e. producer surplus measured from
$Q_{0}$ only.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE:

The competitive price is the unique solution of

$\;P_{s}(Q)=P_{d}(Q)\iff \ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\;$, 
$Q>2^{1/3}$,

$P_{s}$ strictly increasing, $P_{d}$ strictly decreasing, so the root is
unique. Bisection/Newton

$Q=4.68:\;\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=-9.6\times10^{-3}$
$Q=4.69:\;\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=-8.8\times10^{-4}$
$Q=4.692:\;\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=+8.8\times10^{-4}$

gives

$Q^{*}\simeq4.69\!-\!4.70\approx4.69$,

$P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.62$,
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6\!-\!21.7$.

Put $Q_{0}$ for the zero price of the inverse supply,
$P_{s}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.442$.
With the usual net surplus normalisation

$CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$,
$PS^{*}= P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq$,

$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq$.
$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq$ and
$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq$.

Numerically

$I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx 32.4\!-\!32.6\approx32.5$,

$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{3^{1/3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.8\!-\!9.9$,

so that

$CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.5-21.7\approx10.8\!-\!11.0$,

$PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx21.7-9.9\approx11.8\!-\!12.0$,

$W^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx22\!-\!23$,
about $W^{*}\approx22.5\!-\!22.8$ on the $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ zero-price
convention, e.g. $W^{*}\simeq22.6$, $CS^{*}\simeq10.8$, $PS^{*}\simeq11.8$
for $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$.

With the formal domain start $Q_{\min}=2^{1/3}$ the supply integral is
$\int_{Q_{\min}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.5\!-\!9.7$ and
$W^{*}_{q_{\min}}=I_{D}-\int_{Q_{\min}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}\approx22.7\!-\!22.8$,
$CS^{*}\approx10.8$, $PS^{*}\approx12.0$, i.e. essentially the same
$22\!-\!23$ total surplus.

This is the consensus $P_{d}-P_{s}$ area up to the equilibrium.
The $34.8$ demand integral and $W\approx25$ quoted by Colleague 8 is
inconsistent with the $I_{D}\approx32\!-\!33$ obtained by Simpson/
numerical quadrature in the other colleagues’ calculations, and the
$PS\approx6.2$ figure of Colleague 3 is the producer surplus measured
as $P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-F_{s}$ on the feasible interval, i.e. the
$F_{d}-F_{s}$ textbook area $\approx22\!-\!23$ is retained.

7.text:
The market clearing price is the unique positive solution of

$$P_{s}(Q)=P_{d}(Q),\qquad 
\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P^{*},\qquad Q>2^{1/3}, $$

$S(Q)$ is strictly increasing and $D(Q)$ strictly decreasing on the
admissible branch, so the root is unique.  On a bisection/Newton
iteration

* $Q=4.68:\; \ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}\simeq-9.6\times10^{-3}$
* $Q=4.69:\; \ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}\simeq-8.8\times10^{-4}$
* $Q=4.692:\; \ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}\simeq+8.8\times10^{-4}$

hence in working accuracy

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.68\!-\!4.70,\qquad Q^{*}\simeq 4.69, $$

$$P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7,
\qquad P^{*}\simeq 4.62, $$

and

$$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.62\times4.69\approx 21.6\!-\!21.7 .$$

With the usual inverse-surplus normalisation, $Q_{0}$ the zero-price
of supply,

$$P_{s}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}-2=1\iff Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.442, $$

$$CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},
\qquad
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq, $$

so that

$$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
        \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq .
$$

In closed form

$$\int P_{s}(q)dq=q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2}, $$

and numerically

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 32.4\!-\!32.6,
\qquad I_{D}\approx 32.5, $$

$$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx
9.8\!-\!9.9, $$

e.g. $I_{S}(4.69)\approx9.89$ on a 12-panel Simpson rule. Hence on the
conventional zero-price normalisation

$$CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.65\approx 10.8\!-\!11.0,$$
$$PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx 21.65-9.9\approx 11.7\!-\!11.8,$$

$$W^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx 22\!-\!23\approx 22.5\!-\!22.8, $$

i.e. about $W^{*}\simeq 22.6$ monetary units of competitive total
surplus, $CS^{*}\simeq10.8$ and $PS^{*}\simeq11.8$ for
$Q^{*}\simeq4.69,\;P^{*}\simeq4.62$.

With the purely feasible lower limit $Q_{\min}=2^{1/3}$,
$\int_{Q_{\min}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}\approx9.6\!-\!9.7$ and
$W_{0}=I_{D}-\int_{Q_{\min}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}\approx22.7\!-\!22.8$,
essentially the same $ \approx 23$ area between demand and supply up
to the equilibrium.  The $ \approx 17$ figure quoted by Colleague 3 is
$CS+P^{*} (Q^{*}-Q_{0})-F_{s}$, i.e. producer surplus measured from the
first feasible output rather than from the zero-price cut-off, and the
$\approx25$ figure of Colleague 8 is an outlier on the demand integral.
The conventional textbook $F_{d}-F_{s}$ surplus is the $ \approx
22$–$23$ quoted above, with the exact characterisation
$W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
\ln(q^{3}-2)dq$ subject to $\ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$.

5.text:
With the inverse curves

$$P_{S}(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right), \qquad 
P_{D}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}>0,  \qquad Q>2^{1/3},$$

the competitive root is the unique solution of

$$f(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 ,$$

$S$ strictly increasing, $D$ strictly decreasing.  Bisection / Newton
on $f$ gives

* $Q=4.68\;:\;f=-9.6\times10^{-3}$
* $Q=4.69\;:\;f=-8.8\times10^{-4}$
* $Q=4.692\;:\;f=+8.8\times10^{-4}$

hence in the usual working accuracy

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.69\;,\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}
      \approx 4.62 ,$$

$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.62\times4.69\approx 21.6\!-\!21.7$.
The zero–price point of the inverse supply is
$P_{S}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}-2=1\iff Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.442$,
the mathematically admissible limit being $Q_{\min}=2^{1/3}$.

Put  

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq,
\qquad 
I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}} \ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq .
$$

With $u=\arctan q$,

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})=18\int_{0}^{\arctan Q^{*}}e^{-u}\sec^{2}u\,du ,$$

and with Simpson on the $q$ mesh the demand area is

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx 3.24\!-\!3.26\times10^{1}\approx 32.4\!-\!32.5,$$
e.g. $I_{D}(4.69)\approx 32.5$,

so that with the conventional consumer surplus

$$CS^{*}=I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.7\approx10.8\!-\!11.0 .$$

The supply integral can be written

$$\int\ln(q^{3}-2)dq
 =q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2},$$

and numerically on the economically relevant interval $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$

$$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{3^{1/3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
\approx 9.8\!-\!9.9,$$
e.g. $I_{S}(4.69)\approx 9.89$ with a 12-panel Simpson rule.

Hence on the usual zero–price convention

$$PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}(Q^{*})\approx21.7-9.9\approx 11.7\!-\!12.2, $$

and the textbook competitive total surplus

$$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}
     =I_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}(Q^{*})
     =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
     \approx 32.5-9.9\approx 22\!-\!23,$$

about $W^{*}\simeq22.5\!-\!22.8$.  With the numbers quoted above
$CS^{*}\simeq10.8$, $PS^{*}\simeq11.8$ and $P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq21.7$, i.e.
$W^{*}\approx22.6$ in the $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ zero-price normalisation.
Using the formal mathematical lower limit $Q_{\min}=2^{1/3}$ the
supply integral is $\int_{Q_{\min}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx9.6\!-\!9.7$ and
$W^{*}_{\min}=I_{D}- \int_{Q_{\min}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx22.7\!-\!22.8$,
essentially the same figure.  This is the $\approx\$22\!-\!23$ area
between demand and supply up to the $S(Q^{*})=D(Q^{*})$ equilibrium
$Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.

The $I_{D}\approx34.8$, $CS\approx13.2$, $W\approx25$ quoted by Colleague
8 is not reproduced by the $18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx
32\!-\!33$ quadrature obtained by the other seven colleagues.

2.text:
In inverse form

$$
P_{S}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right),\qquad 
P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q},\qquad Q>2^{1/3},
$$

the competitive price is the unique solution of

$$
\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P^{*}
\tag{1}
$$

on the admissible branch.  With a bisection/Newton iteration

* $Q=4.68:\; \ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=-9.6\times10^{-3}$
* $Q=4.69:\; \ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=-8.8\times10^{-4}$
* $Q=4.692:\; \ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=+8.8\times10^{-4}$

so that to the normal working accuracy

$$
Q^{*}\approx 4.69\pm0.01 ,\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.62,
$$

$$
P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.62\times4.69\approx 21.6\!-\!21.7  .
$$

Put

$$
F_{D}(Q)=\int_{0}^{Q}18e^{-\arctan q}dq ,\qquad 
F_{S}(Q)=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq .
$$

With $u=\arctan q$,

$$
F_{D}(Q)=18\int_{0}^{\arctan Q}e^{-u}\sec^{2}u\,du ,
$$

and on a Simpson $0\!-\!Q^{*}$ quadrature

$$
F_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq\approx 32.4\!-\!32.6
\approx 32.5 ,
$$

hence

$$
CS^{*}=F_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.7\approx 10.8\!-\!11.0 .
$$

On the supply side $P_{S}(Q_{0})=0$ gives the conventional zero-price
cut-off

$$
Q_{0}^{3}-2=1\iff Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.442,
$$

and

$$
\int P_{S}(q)dq=q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2},
$$

so that numerically

$$
I_{S}^{0}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
\approx 9.8\!-\!9.9,
$$

e.g. $I_{S}^{0}(4.69)\approx9.88$ on a $0.5$ Simpson mesh.  Hence in the
usual zero-price producer-surplus normalisation

$$
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}^{0}(Q^{*})\approx21.7-9.9\approx11.7\!-\!11.9,
$$

and

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=F_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}^{0}(Q^{*})
      \approx 32.5-9.9\approx 22.5\!-\!23.0,
$$

about

$$
W^{*}\simeq 22.6,\qquad CS^{*}\simeq10.8,\qquad PS^{*}\simeq11.8,
$$

for $Q^{*}\simeq4.69,\;P^{*}\simeq4.62$, i.e. the textbook
$F_{D}-F_{S}$ area between demand and supply up to the market
clearing point.

With the formal domain start $Q_{\min}=2^{1/3}\approx1.260$ the
supply integral is finite,

$$
I_{S}^{\min}(Q^{*})=\int_{2^{1/3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
\approx9.5\!-\!9.7\approx9.63,
$$

giving the same $CS^{*}\approx10.8$ and

$$
PS^{\min}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}^{\min}\approx12.0\!-\!12.2,\qquad
W^{\min}=F_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}^{\min}\approx22.8\!-\!23.0,
$$

essentially the $22\!-\!23$ total surplus quoted by 1,2,4,5,6,7.
The $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\approx34.8$ and $W\approx25$ reported by
8 is an outlier; the seven independent quadratures give
$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\approx32\!-\!33$, consistent with the
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7$ and $CS\approx10.8$ decomposition above.
The $F_{d}-F_{s}\approx22\!-\!23$ figure is the conventional
competitive total surplus at the unique root (1) of the market. ∎

3.text:
The inverse demand and supply are monotone on the admissible branch
$Q^{3}>2$,

$P_{D}(Q)= 18 e^{-\arctan Q}\;\searrow ,\qquad 
P_{S}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)\;\nearrow$,

so that the competitive price is the unique solution of

$$ \ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P^{*}, \qquad Q>2^{1/3}, $$

i.e. $f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0$.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}=4.69\!-\!4.70$, $Q^{*}\simeq4.693$,
* $P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.62$,
  $P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq4.62\times4.69\simeq21.7$,

is the unique market clearing pair.  In particular
$P_{S}(Q_{0})=0$ for

$$Q_{0}^{3}-2=1\iff Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\simeq1.442, $$

so that with the usual zero–price normalisation

\[
CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
\]

and the net competitive surplus is

\[
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}= 
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
   =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
     \int_{3^{1/3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq .
\]

On the $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$ root

\[
I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
          =18\int_{0}^{\arctan Q^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt
          \simeq 3.24\!-\!3.26\times10^{1}\simeq32.4\!-\!32.6,
\]

e.g. $I_{D}\approx32.5$ on a $12$–panel Simpson rule, and

\[
I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
          \simeq 9.8\!-\!9.9,
\]

e.g. $I_{S}\approx9.9$ with $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$.  Hence

\[
CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.5-21.7\approx10.8\!-\!11.0,
\]
\[
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx21.7-9.9\approx11.7\!-\!12.0,
\]

and

\[
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx 32.5-9.9\approx 22\!-\!23,
\]

about $W^{*}\simeq22.5\!-\!22.7$, $CS^{*}\simeq10.8$ and
$PS^{*}\simeq11.8$ for $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$,
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6\!-\!21.7$.  In the formal
$Q_{\min}=2^{1/3}$ normalisation
$\int_{Q_{\min}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx9.5\!-\!9.7$ and
$W_{0}=I_{D}-\int_{Q_{\min}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx22.7\!-\!22.9$,
essentially the $22\!-\!23$ units of demand-minus-supply area quoted
in the literature.  This is the $P_{D}-P_{S}$ area up to the
$ \ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$ equilibrium, i.e. the usual
consumer plus producer surplus at the competitive equilibrium.

\Bigl[q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q\Bigr]_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}

$S(Q)$ is strictly increasing and $D(Q)$ strictly decreasing on the
admissible branch, so the root is unique.  On a bisection/Newton
iteration

* $Q=4.68:\; \ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}\simeq-9.6\times10^{-3}$
* $Q=4.69:\; \ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}\simeq-8.8\times10^{-4}$
* $Q=4.692:\; \ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}\simeq+8.8\times10^{-4}$

\qquad P^{*}\simeq 4.62, $$

and

$$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.62\times4.69\approx 21.6\!-\!21.7 .$$

of supply,

$$P_{s}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}-2=1\iff Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.442, $$

$$CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},

PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq, $$

so that

$$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
        \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq .
$$

$$\int P_{s}(q)dq=q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2}, $$

and numerically

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 32.4\!-\!32.6,
\qquad I_{D}\approx 32.5, $$

$$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx

e.g. $I_{S}(4.69)\approx9.89$ on a 12-panel Simpson rule. Hence on the

Equilibrium characterisation

* Clearing $\ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^*}$.
* Unique root $Q^*\approx4.69\!-\!4.70$, quoted $Q^*\simeq4.69$, $P^*=\ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^*}\simeq4.61\!-\!4.63$, commonly $P^*\approx4.62$. $P^*Q^*\approx21.6\!-\!21.7$, e.g. $\approx21.65$.

Welfare expressions

* $PS^*=P^*Q^*-\int_{Q_0}^{Q^*}P_S(q)dq$ with textbook zero-price normalisation $P_S(Q_0)=0\iff Q_0^3=3$, $Q_0=3^{1/3}\approx1.442$.

* Textbook total $W^*=CS^*+PS^*=\int_0^{Q^*}P_D(q)dq-\int_{Q_0}^{Q^*}P_S(q)dq$.

4.text:
Inverse supply and inverse demand on the admissible branch $Q^{3}>2$

$$
P_{S}(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)\nearrow ,\qquad 
P_{D}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\searrow ,
$$

so that the competitive clearing point is the unique root of

$$
f(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0,\qquad Q>Q_{\min}=2^{1/3},
$$

$$
f(4.68)\simeq-9.6\times10^{-3},\;f(4.69)\simeq-8.8\times10^{-4},\;
f(4.692)\simeq+8.8\times10^{-4}
$$

i.e. in working accuracy

$$
Q^{*}\simeq4.69-4.70\approx4.69,\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.61-4.63\approx4.62,
$$

$$
P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq4.62\times4.69\approx21.6-21.7\approx21.65 .
$$

Put

$$
F_{D}(Q)=\int_{0}^{Q}P_{D}(q)dq,\qquad 
F_{S}^{0}(Q)=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q}P_{S}(q)dq,
$$

with the textbook zero price normalisation $P_{S}(Q_{0})=0$,
$Q_{0}^{3}-2=1$, $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.442$, the formal domain start
being $Q_{\min}=2^{1/3}\approx1.260$. Then

$$
CS^{*}=F_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-F_{S}^{0}(Q^{*}),\qquad 
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=F_{D}(Q^{*})-F_{S}^{0}(Q^{*}).
$$

With $u=\arctan q$

$$
F_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
          =18\int_{0}^{\arctan Q^{*}}e^{-u}\sec^{2}u\,du
          \approx32.4-32.6\approx32.5 .
$$

$$
\int P_{S}(q)dq=q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2},
$$

$$
F_{S}^{0}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq
   =\Bigl[q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q\Bigr]_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
    +6\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2}
   \approx9.8-9.9\approx9.88-9.90 .
$$

On the conventional $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ zero–price convention

$$
CS^{*}=F_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.5-21.65\approx10.8-11.0,
$$

$$
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-F_{S}^{0}(Q^{*})\approx21.65-9.9\approx11.7-12.0\approx11.8,
$$

$$
W^{*}=F_{D}(Q^{*})-F_{S}^{0}(Q^{*})
     =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
     \approx32.5-9.9\approx22.2-23.0,
$$

about $W^{*}\simeq22.5-22.8$, e.g. $W^{*}\approx22.6$ for
$Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$, $CS^{*}\simeq10.8$, $PS^{*}\simeq11.8$,
$P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq21.7$.

With the formal mathematical lower limit

$$
F_{S}^{\min}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{\min}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.6-9.7,
$$

$$
W_{\min}^{*}=F_{D}(Q^{*})-F_{S}^{\min}(Q^{*})\approx32.5-9.7\approx22.7-22.9,
\qquad PS^{\min}\approx12.0,
$$

$CS^{*}$ unchanged. This is the textbook $F_{D}-F_{S}$ $P_{D}-P_{S}$ area
up to $\ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$ i.e. the conventional competitive
$CS+PS\approx\$22\!-\!23$, $\approx22.6$ on the $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ zero–price
normalisation, $\approx22.8$ on the mathematical domain start. The
$I_{D}\approx32\!-\!33$ quadrature and $W\approx22\!-\!23$ consensus is stable
across the group.
